title: The Last American Iron Lung Patient Just Died — Marking the End of a Pre-Vaccine Era
hook: Martha Lillard survived 73 years after polio paralyzed her at age 5, breathing every night inside an iron lung. Her death closes a chapter vaccines quietly ended.
key_points: Martha Lillard contracted polio at age 5, which paralyzed her from the neck down; doctors told her she wouldn't live past 20 — she lived to 78.
She died June 26, 2026, in Oklahoma, the last known American still dependent on an iron lung for polio.
An iron lung is a cylindrical chamber that mechanically forces air in and out of the lungs by manipulating air pressure around the body, letting someone with paralyzed breathing muscles survive.
Before vaccines, polio caused thousands of paralysis cases every year in the U.S.; vaccination eliminated the disease domestically by 1979.
content_html: Martha Lillard was 5 years old when polio paralyzed her from the neck down. Doctors told her she wouldn't live past 20. She lived to 78 — sleeping every night of her adult life inside an iron lung.
extra_html: Lillard, who died June 26, 2026, in Oklahoma, was the last known American still dependent on an iron lung for polio, a machine that mechanically forces air in and out of the lungs by manipulating pressure around the body, letting someone with paralyzed breathing muscles keep breathing. She spent her final two years in the machine nearly around the clock, while still finding time to write poems, compose songs, and volunteer with animal rescue. Before vaccines, polio paralyzed thousands of Americans a year; vaccination campaigns eliminated the disease domestically by 1979, and Lillard's death marks the quiet close of that pre-vaccine chapter. As her sister put it, "since she's the last one, we don't need that anymore" — the machine's usefulness ended along with the disease that made it necessary.

related.title: Vaccines
related.hook: A vaccine is a training session for your immune system — it learns to beat a dangerous pathogen using a harmless preview, so the real fight is already half-won.

related.title: How Infections Spread
related.hook: Germs can't fly to a new host on their own — they hitch rides on coughs, hands, food, water, and insects. Break the ride, and you break the chain of infection.
